previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of post-polio syndrome, CAD s/p CABG, and depression was admitted for generalized weakness and recurrent falls. She presented after calling EMS due to severe weakness and fear of falling, with recent psychosocial stressors including the loss of her husband and pet. Evaluation revealed a urinary tract infection with E. coli on culture, despite being asymptomatic for typical urinary symptoms. She was treated with IV ceftriaxone and transitioned to oral cefpodoxime. Mild pulmonary edema was noted on imaging but required no intervention. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia remained at baseline. Blood cultures remained negative. Physical therapy recommended inpatient rehabilitation for deconditioning, which the patient accepted. She was discharged to an extended care facility with plans to complete her antibiotic course, continue home medications including sertraline for depression, and follow up on pending concerns with her PCP.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MRI THORACIC AND LUMBAR PT6 MR SPINE.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with lower back pain, bilateral great toe
numbness.  Evaluate for cauda equina syndrome or cord compression

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal imaging was performed with T2, T1, and STIR technique,
followed by axial T2 imaging.

COMPARISON:  ___ abdomen and pelvis CT.
___ lumbar spine MRI.

FINDINGS:


THORACIC SPINE:
The T4, T5, and T6 vertebral bodies are partially fused anteriorly, likely
congenital (series 13, image 10).  A Schmorl's node along the superior
endplate of T12 with adjacent focal STIR hyperintense signal is unchanged. 
Mild compression deformities of the T10 and T11 vertebral bodies without
associated marrow edema are unchanged compared to prior examinations. 
Thoracic spine alignment is preserved.  There is no spinal canal or neural
foraminal narrowing in the thoracic spine.  The thoracic spinal cord is normal
in caliber and signal intensity.

LUMBAR SPINE:
Compression fracture of the L1 vertebral body is new compared to the prior MRI
of ___ but unchanged since the abdominal CT of ___
(series 18, image 10).  Retropulsion into the spinal canal resulting in mild
to moderate focal narrowing is grossly unchanged (series 18, image 9; series
21, image 3).  There is residual STIR hyperintense signal in the L1 vertebral
body and the adjacent intervertebral discs.

Compression fracture of the L2 vertebral body with approximately 50% loss of
height has slightly progressed since the prior study of ___, but
is probably similar compared to the CT of ___.  Residual marrow
edema in the L2 vertebral body has overall decreased compared to the prior
study of ___, however there is a small focus of intense STIR
hyperintense signal along the inferior endplate anteriorly which could
represent an acute injury or alternatively ___ type 1 degenerative changes
(series 14, image 5).

There is increased irregularity and the STIR hyperintense signal along the
superior endplate of L3, with mild loss of height which is new compared to the
prior MRI of ___ and CT of ___, likely representing
an acute to subacute compression fracture.  There is no retropulsion.

Mild compression fracture of the L4 vertebral body is grossly unchanged since
the prior study of ___ however marrow edema has substantially
decreased.

There is new extensive marrow edema in the L5 vertebral body with mild loss of
height that is new compared to the prior examinations and consistent with an
acute or subacute compression fracture.  There is no retropulsion.

Previously noted edema in the L1-L2 interspinous ligament is no longer
appreciated.  There is no abnormal T2/STIR hyperintense signal in the
posterior ligamentous complex.  Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
and ligamentum flavum are grossly intact.


At T12-L1, there is mild-to-moderate narrowing of the spinal canal as a result
of bony retropulsion of the L1 vertebral body.  There is moderate neural
foraminal narrowing bilaterally.

At L1-L2, disc bulge and marginal osteophytes result in mild narrowing of the
spinal canal.  Bilateral neural foraminal narrowing is mild.

At L2-L3, there is mild diffuse disc bulge and mild spondylosis with Schmorl's
nodes, causing mild bilateral neural foraminal narrowing, slightly more
pronounced on the right (image 11, series 21).

At L3-L4, there is disc desiccation and mild diffuse disc bulge, causing mild
bilateral neural foraminal narrowing, right greater than left, apparently
contacting the traversing nerve roots bilaterally, no significant spinal canal
narrowing is identified.

At L4-L5, disc bulging and marginal osteophytes results in mild narrowing of
the spinal canal.  There is moderate to severe right and mild-to-moderate left
neural foraminal narrowing.

At L5-S1, there is a disc bulge with no appreciable spinal canal narrowing. 
There is moderate to severe bilateral neural foraminal narrowing.

The distal spinal cord is normal in caliber and signal intensity.  Conus
medullaris terminates at L1-2.  Nerve roots of the cauda equina are otherwise
unremarkable.

There is no paraspinal or epidural fluid collection.

IMPRESSION:


1. Severe compression fracture of the L1 vertebral body with retropulsion
resulting in mild-to-moderate narrowing of the spinal canal is grossly
unchanged since the prior abdominal CT of ___.  There is mild
residual marrow edema.
2. Bone marrow edema along the superior endplate of L3 and entire body of L5,
with mild interval loss of height as compared to the prior studies is
consistent with acute to subacute compression fractures without retropulsion.
3. New intense focal marrow edema along the inferior endplate of L2 probably
represents an acute on chronic compression fracture, although the overall
moderate loss of height associated with this vertebral body is grossly
unchanged, there is no retropulsion.
4. There is no evidence of cord compression or significant lumbar spinal canal
narrowing.
5. Multilevel neural foraminal narrowing as described above is moderate to
severe at right L4-5 and bilateral L5-S1, slightly progressed compared to the
prior examination.
6. Multiple thoracic compression fractures appear chronic.
